The penultimate MEX theorem excludes every past diagonal from yyy; it does not assert that yyy itself is diagonal. Thus the journal witness cannot be a seed or the host's birth diagonal. F=[max⁡(h+1,m+1), r−2]. \mathcal F=[\max(h+1,m+1),\,r-2]. F=[max(h+1,m+1),r−2].

A label y∈Fy\in\mathcal Fy∈F was absent in every row before h−1h-1h−1, whose maximum is at most mmm, and is not a diagonal seed. The birth diagonals r−1,r+1r-1,r+1r−1,r+1 and later diagonals are also outside this interval. Therefore it is a blocker, and the unique row-(h−1)(h-1)(h−1) service host kyk_yky​ is the only older host whose row-hhh journal contains yyy. Each such journal contains at most one F\mathcal FF-label.

If a larger current F\mathcal FF-label zzz precedes a smaller yyy, the larger recomputed cell's MEX needs yyy in its journal, because the unique current yyy is later. Its host is necessarily kyk_yky​. Thus any smaller label has at most one larger predecessor, and any larger label has at most one smaller successor. No value can have both an incoming and outgoing inversion, because the resulting length-two descending chain creates a second inversion at its first/last value. An inverted pair with a numerical intermediate value creates a second inversion at one endpoint, according to whether the intermediate is before or after the larger value. Hence inversions are disjoint pairs of numerically adjacent labels. The subsequence is the increasing list up to those swaps; other labels may interleave physically.

For h=1h=1h=1, the literal tight case has r=2r=2r=2 and empty F\mathcal FF. For h=2h=2h=2, tightness would force r=3r=3r=3, but 3 is the already-born diagonal d(1)d(1)d(1), so cannot be a death blocker. Column zero is immortal. These cover the small cases without applying the q≥3q\ge3q≥3 terminal lemma below its domain. Nothing says every physical column increases by one.
